entries.title: Ezekiel 4:1
segments:
A tile; the large tiles of Babylon were commonly used for inscriptions and drawings. 
 
When nations and cities refuse to be corrected by God's chastisements, he will multiply his judgments against them until they are utterly destroyed.  No human power can avail to loose the bands which he lays upon the workers of iniquity.

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:2
segments: Lay siege against it; that is, portray a siege.  The final siege of Jerusalem is here meant.  Ezekiel began to prophesy in the fifth year of Zedekiah; consequently six years before the last capture of the city by Nebuchadnezzar.  With the exception of his vision of the temple,
, the great body of his prophecies was delivered during the intervening period.  It is not till
that he records his reception of the news that the city was smitten.

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:3
segments: For a wall of iron; this seems to be a symbol of God's wrath arrayed against Jerusalem in the form of a siege.  For the meaning of iron as a symbol, see

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:4
segments:
vv 4-6. 
 
  Lie thou; the prophet himself now represents the people of Israel and Judah. 
 
  The years of their iniquity--the number of the days; the meaning is, that each day represents a year. 
 
  Three hundred and ninety days--forty days; the interpretation of these numbers is uncertain. According to some, the forty days correspond to the forty years' wandering of the Israelites in the wilderness, and the sum of the two numbers, four hundred and thirty days, to the four hundred and thirty years of servitude in Egypt,

; meaning that God will repeat to his covenant people the chastisements inflicted upon their fathers.  Others understand by the three hundred and ninety days, the three hundred and ninety years from the establishment of idolatry in Israel by Jeroboam to the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar; and by the forty days, forty of the last years of the kingdom of Judah, when idolatry abounded in it.

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:7
segments: Uncovered; as ready for hostile action against Jerusalem.  Here, as in
, the prophet acts as God's representative.

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:8
segments: Lay bands upon thee; to signify that Judah and Israel cannot escape the coming judgments which the prophet thus represents.

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:10
segments:
vv 10-11. 
 
  By weight--by measure; a scanty allowance of food and drink, dealt out by weight and measure, as in time of famine.  A shekel was something more than half an ounce; a hin was about ten pints.

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:12
segments: With dung; that is, dung for fuel; indicating the extreme scarcity of fuel in the city.  By using this unclean substance for fuel, the bread itself would become defiled, that is, unclean, according to the distinctions of the Mosaic law.  Compare

entries.title: Ezekiel 4:15
segments: Cow's dung; a common fuel in eastern countries.
